newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore bionics centre comes to aid of Asia's deaf.
newsitem.headline: Singapore bionics centre comes to aid of Asia's deaf.

text.p: Breakthrough "bionic" implant technology could help some of the estimated 10,000 children born profoundly deaf each year in Southeast Asia to hear and lead normal lives, a pioneering surgeon said on Monday.

Hi-tech electronic implants, identifying speech rather than just sound, combined with new speech therapy techniques offer real hope to the deaf, William Gibson, surgeon and head of Australia's Cochlear Implants International Pty Ltd (CII), told a news conference.
"This is a revolution," Gibson said at the launch of a new CII centre, based at Singapore's Mount Elizabeth Hospital Ltd.
"Ten years ago it would have been undreamed of that deaf children could hear and speak so well that they could go through to regular schools," he said.

"The best we could have hoped for would have been to teach them sign language, read lips and perhaps learn a word or two. A child did not have great prospects," said Gibson, who pioneered the use of the implants in small children.

CII Singapore was launched with the help of Ming Hui Tan from Johor Bahru in Malaysia, who was able to hear the words "happy birthday" for the first time on Monday as she celebrated with her family after the news conference.

Gibson said speech was a vital economic tool. About 60 percent of Australians taught sign language as their primary communication form never gain useful employment with the remainder trapped in low paid, menial jobs, he said.

He said that with the Australia $70,000 (US$54,400) implant -- an external speech processor with decoder and electrode placed in the bones in the ear -- and therapy, prospects for deaf children were never better.

Andrew Kendrick, a speech therapist and CII general manager in Singapore, described the implant as a "miracle device", saying "the ability to be totally incorporated into the hearing world is about 90 percent".

Despite the high price tag, Mount Elizabeth Hospital general manager Joshua Goh said he expected a team of six to eight surgeons plus several locally-trained speech therapists to be treating as many as 40 patients per year through CII Singapore.
"There are already 15 to 20 children with implants in the region waiting for therapy," Goh said.

Having a centre in Singapore would help provide pre-implant assessments, follow-up therapy and avoid long spells apart from parents for children undergoing treatment, which can take as long as one year.
The implants are designed to last 100 years and with improvements in biotechnology, Gibson said upgrades offering significant enhancements could be available at relatively low cost every 10 years.
"The future for deaf children is going to get better and better," he said.
